text: A prayer of David. Hear my just cause, LORD; listen to my cry; give ear to my prayer— it comes from lips without deceit.
Let my vindication come from your presence; let your eyes see what is right.
You have tested my heart and examined me by night; you have refined me and found nothing wrong. I have resolved that my mouth will not sin.
As for the deeds of men, by the word of your lips I have kept myself from the ways of the violent.

versions.text: As for what people do—by the word of your lips I have kept clear of the paths of the violent.
versions.explanation: 'What people do' is vague and the dash breaks the rhythm; 'the deeds of men' better matches לִפְעֻלּוֹת אָדָם and reads more smoothly aloud.

text: Hold my steps steady on your paths, that my feet may not slip.

versions.text: My steps hold fast to your ways; my feet have not stumbled.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew verb תָּמֹךְ is an imperative (or infinitive absolute used as imperative) addressed to God, and בַּל־נָמוֹטּוּ expresses purpose/result ('so that my footsteps do not slip'). The current rendering turns a petition into a self-affirming statement, which loses the prayer's dependence on God.

text: I call on you, O God, for you answer me; turn your ear to me and hear my words.

versions.text: I call on you, O God, for you will answer me; turn your ear to me and hear my words.
versions.explanation: Minor nuance: the imperfect תַעֲנֵנִי here expresses confident present reality ('you answer me') as much as future; 'you answer me' preserves the psalmist's settled trust. Optional refinement.

text: Show the wonder of your faithful love, Savior of all who take refuge in you; by your right hand save them from those who rise against them.

versions.text: Show the wonder of your mercy, Savior of all who take refuge at your right hand from those who rise against them.
versions.explanation: The phrase בִּימִינֶךָ ('by your right hand') modifies the saving action, not the place of refuge. Attaching it to 'take refuge' misconstrues the Hebrew and creates an awkward, ambiguous clause when read aloud.

text: Guard me as the apple of your eye; hide me in the shadow of your wings
from the wicked who assault me, from my deadly enemies who close in on me.
Their hearts are sealed in fat; their mouths speak with arrogance.
They have tracked down our steps; now they surround us, their eyes fixed to bring us to the ground.

versions.text: They have tracked me down; now they surround me, their eyes fixed to bring me to the ground.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew (following the qere סְבָבוּנוּ and the suffix on אַשֻּׁרֵינוּ) is first person plural: 'our steps ... they have surrounded us.' The translation shifts to the singular without warrant and also drops the explicit reference to 'steps,' which links this verse to the 'steps/feet' imagery of verse 5.

text: He is like a lion hungry for prey, like a young lion crouching in hiding.

versions.text: They are like a lion hungry for prey, like a young lion crouching in hiding.
versions.explanation: דִּמְיֹנוֹ ('his likeness') is singular, focusing on one chief adversary. The plural 'they' also leaves the singular pronouns of verse 13 ('Confront him, bring him down') without an antecedent when the psalm is read aloud.

text: Rise up, LORD! Confront him, bring him down; rescue my life from the wicked by your sword.

versions.text: Rise up, LORD! Confront him, bring him down; deliver my life from the wicked with your sword.
versions.explanation: 'Deliver ... with your sword' is ambiguous when read aloud (it can sound as though the wicked holds the sword). 'Rescue ... by your sword' clarifies that the sword is God's instrument, matching מֵרָשָׁע חַרְבֶּךָ.

text: Deliver me by your hand, LORD, from men of this world whose portion is in this life. You fill their bellies with what you have stored up; their children have their fill, and they leave the rest to their little ones.

versions.text: Deliver me by your hand, LORD, from mortals—from mortals of this world whose portion is in this life. You fill their bellies with what you have stored up; their children have their fill, and they leave the rest to their little ones.
versions.explanation: The repeated 'from mortals—from mortals' reproduces a Hebrew repetition that sounds stilted in oral English; condensing keeps the sense while improving flow.

text: But I, in righteousness, will see your face; when I awake, I will be satisfied with your likeness.
